preamble: In this anniversary puzzle eight solutions are of a kind and not further defined

clue.text: Weaver has to drink a toast

parts.note: Nick Bottom is the weaver in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream
's is the contracted form of has
to sup is to drink, split across the enumeration

explanation.surface: A weaver is obliged to knock back a celebratory toast.
explanation.walkthrough: The weaver is Bottom from A Midsummer Night's Dream; 'has' shrinks to 'S and 'to drink' is SUP, so the S does double duty at the word break.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the exclamation people call out as they raise glasses and drain them, so it serves as a toast.

clue.text: Pancake made by old car manufacturer in Italy

parts.note: British Leyland, the defunct UK carmaker
taken as written
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A pancake turned out by a vintage carmaker's Italian factory.
explanation.walkthrough: BL stands for British Leyland, the state-owned group behind the Mini and Austin cars; I is the country code on Italian number plates.
explanation.definitionFit: Blinis are small Russian buckwheat griddle cakes, often served with caviar, so they are a type of pancake.

clue.text: Train's running on time!

indicators.note: running here means operating loosely, so the letters move about into a new order

parts.note: the word with its apostrophe ignored
T is the abbreviation for time, added on

explanation.surface: A cheer that the railway service is punctual for once.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no definition: the preamble says eight answers are of one kind, and this is one of them, the Ford Transit van.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ford Transit is the long-running van made by the company whose founder this anniversary puzzle celebrates.

clue.text: Huge islet over in old Roman port

parts.note: OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something over flips it end to end

parts.note: an ait is a small river island, as on the Thames

explanation.surface: An enormous island sitting in an ancient Roman harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: OS (outsize) is a British label for large clothing sizes; an ait or eyot is a crossword favourite for a little island in a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostia was the harbour city at the mouth of the Tiber that served ancient Rome as its seaport.

clue.text: Heads from St Pancras, carrying my 10

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it inside, so one piece holds another
the heads of words are their opening letters, so only those are kept

parts.note: first letters of the two words
cor! is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'
the digits 1 and 0 read as the letters I and O

explanation.surface: Leaders setting off from a London station with the speaker's ten in tow.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' is not a cross-reference: read as letters it is IO. Like the other theme answers it has no definition, and is the Ford Scorpio executive car.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scorpio was Ford of Europe's large executive saloon of the 1980s and 1990s, one of the puzzle's eight Ford models.

clue.text: Clergyman in China has 10 that's replaced 20

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another is placed inside it

parts.note: china plate is Cockney rhyming slang for mate, a pal
Rev is short for Reverend, a clergyman's title

indicators.note: letters that have been replaced are put back in different positions

parts.note: the number written out as a word

explanation.surface: A churchman in China has ten of something that took the place of twenty.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference 20 is the definition: 20-down is POPULAR. In rhyming slang 'china plate' means mate, so china is a crossword standard for PAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Something widespread and commonly found is prevalent, just as a widely liked or common thing is popular.

clue.text: Relative from around Dagenham area originally, leaving Spanish city (ninth of theme)

indicators.note: whatever is leaving goes away, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: Granada, the Andalusian city of the Alhambra

indicators.note: what something was originally is its start, so only opening letters count

parts.note: first letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A relation who moved from somewhere near Dagenham, leaving behind a home in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking ADA off the end of GRANADA leaves the answer. The bracket notes that the Ford Granada would have been a ninth theme car; Dagenham, east of London, housed Ford's huge British factory.
explanation.definitionFit: Gran is the familiar British name for a grandmother, so it is a family member, a relative.

clue.text: Bearing clubs, go and seek out reptiles

indicators.note: to bear something is to carry it, so the outer letters hold an extra one
out can mean disordered or wrong, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games

explanation.surface: Armed with clubs, set off to hunt down some lizards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go and seek' looks like an instruction but only lends its letters; the 'and' links the two words of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Geckos are small climbing lizards found in warm countries, and lizards are reptiles, so the plural fits.

clue.text: Means of transporting a mineral over to Nepal, perhaps

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down entry, flipping over turns the letters upside down
perhaps marks a possible version, so these letters may come out in another order

parts.note: ore is mineral-bearing rock
the country's name, used for its letters

explanation.surface: How to ship some mineral across to Nepal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks how to carry ore to Nepal, and the answer would indeed do it; the definition is just the opening words.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft carries people and goods from place to place, so it is a means of transport.

clue.text: Orlando's coriander left in 17, sadly

indicators.note: something done sadly goes badly, so the letters end up in a sorry jumble

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left
the answer to 17-down, the Ford model

explanation.surface: A Florida man's herb abandoned in his car, which is a shame.
explanation.walkthrough: Orlando, in Florida, signals an American word: the herb Britons call coriander goes by its Spanish name in the US.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans name the leaves of the coriander plant by this Spanish word, so it is the US term for that herb.

clue.text: Horn used in street after heading for Euston

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its opening letter, which leads off here

parts.note: first letter of the London station

indicators.note: something used in another thing is put inside it

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street
cor is French for horn, as in cor anglais

explanation.surface: Someone sounds a car horn on the road outside a London railway terminus.
explanation.walkthrough: A theme answer, so no definition: this is the Ford Escort. The opening letter of Euston comes after the street-with-horn piece in the clue order but first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Escort was Ford's best-selling small family car in Britain for decades, one of the eight Ford models in the theme.

clue.text: Half of "Wolfie" Smith's Tooting army, initially

indicators.note: taking half of a word means losing the other half of its letters

parts.note: the second half of the nickname

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of each word that follows

parts.note: first letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A nod to Citizen Smith, the 1970s British sitcom whose hero Wolfie led the Tooting Popular Front, a tiny revolutionary army.
explanation.walkthrough: A theme answer with no definition: the Ford Fiesta supermini. Tooting is a district of south London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Fiesta is Ford's small hatchback, launched in 1976 and long Britain's top-selling car, so it belongs to the theme.

clue.text: Head of state avoids thick fogs, for starters

indicators.note: to avoid something is to steer clear of it, so those letters are left out

parts.note: a pea-souper is a dense yellowish London fog
ER, Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A president steers clear of dense fog, for a start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for starters' looks like the usual signal for first letters, but 'starters' is the definition, meaning first courses. The Queen as ER is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Bowls of thick pea broth are served as first courses at a meal, and a first course is a starter in British usage.

clue.text: Quiet jail

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to silence someone, or the command to be silent
second meaning: to lock someone away, imprison

explanation.walkthrough: Both words are verbs here: to make someone hush, and to confine them behind bars.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to stop someone talking and to lock someone up somewhere they cannot get out.

clue.text: King's Cross, as subject of anniversary

parts.note: England has had eight kings called Henry
to ford a river is to cross it by wading

explanation.surface: King's Cross, the London railway terminus, as the topic of a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of King's is just glue: the king is followed by the crossing. The puzzle appeared on the 150th anniversary of the carmaker's birth in July 1863.
explanation.definitionFit: The American industrialist who founded the motor company was born in 1863, so this puzzle marked his anniversary.

clue.text: Caught setter going in for stud for nose

indicators.note: things going in another enter it and end up inside

parts.note: pro means in favour of, for
a boss is a stud or knob on a surface
C is the cricket scoring abbreviation for caught
the setter refers to themself as I

explanation.surface: The setter, caught, goes in for a horse at stud, for some reason, nose first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for stud' is read as two separate pieces placed side by side. A boss is a raised ornamental knob or stud, as on a shield or a ceiling.
explanation.definitionFit: A proboscis is an elongated nose or snout, as of an elephant, and jokingly any large human nose.

clue.text: Lines inside coast suffering bilateral erosion abroad

indicators.note: worn away on both sides means the ends are lost
something inside another is held within it

parts.note: the word with its outer letters worn off, C at one end and T at the other
lines of poetry are verse

explanation.surface: A shoreline being eaten away at both ends, somewhere in a foreign land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bilateral erosion' takes one letter off the front and one off the back of coast, leaving OAS to hold the lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe being in or going to a foreign country across the sea, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Amusing story one acted out

indicators.note: out can mean in disarray or wrong, so the letters get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A funny tale that someone performed as a little play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'acted out' reads as a phrasal verb, but 'acted' belongs to the fodder and 'out' alone does the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: An anecdote is a short entertaining tale about a real incident or person, usually told in conversation.

clue.text: Irish county's detailed model of 13 part 2 in centre of Ballinascarty

indicators.note: de-tailed means with its tail removed, so the final letter goes

parts.note: Cork, the Irish county, minus its last letter
part 2 of 13-down's answer is the company; its famous Model T
taken as written

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter, the only one kept

parts.note: the seventh of thirteen letters

explanation.surface: A detailed scale model of a Ford car made in a County Cork village.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Ford's father came from Ballinascarty in County Cork, which is why the surface sits there. A theme answer with no definition: the Ford Cortina.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cortina was Ford's family saloon that topped British sales charts through the 1970s, so it belongs to the theme.

clue.text: Tranquil fellow in rough sea, not initially blue

indicators.note: not having its start means the first letter is dropped
one thing in another sits inside it
rough means choppy and disturbed, so the letters are tossed about

parts.note: taken as written
blue without its first letter
F is the abbreviation for fellow

explanation.surface: A calm man adrift in a stormy sea, refusing at first to feel low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rough' governs both sea and the shortened blue, and the fellow sits inside the mixed letters. Tranquil and rough sea pull against each other in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An old literary word for restful or peaceful, as in Keats's 'easeful Death', so it matches calm and serene.

clue.text: Valved pipe — favourite part of 13 part 2, perhaps

parts.note: a tap is a pipe fitted with a valve
a teacher's pet is a favourite

explanation.surface: A pipe with a valve, the best-loved component of a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 part 2 is the second word of 13-down, the carmaker's name, so the definition means a component of a Ford car, with 'perhaps' showing it is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A tappet is a sliding rod in an engine that pushes a valve open, found in any car engine, Fords included.

clue.text: University in London area

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it

parts.note: Poplar is a district in the East End of London
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A college located in some part of London.
explanation.walkthrough: A theme answer with no definition: the Ford Popular, a cheap 1950s British family car. Poplar is an East London district near Canary Wharf.
explanation.definitionFit: The Popular was Ford of Britain's budget small car of the 1950s, sold as the cheapest car on the market.

clue.text: Sporty car's first one produced for islanders

indicators.note: something produced is made up or manufactured from the materials given

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: first picks out only the opening letter of the word

parts.note: opening letter of the word
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: The first model of a sports car built for people living on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sporty car' hints at the Ford Capri, which this answer nearly contains, but 'Sporty' is anagram fodder and 'car' gives only its initial.
explanation.definitionFit: People from Cyprus, an island nation in the eastern Mediterranean, are islanders by definition.

clue.text: Material in partly emptied train about to leave a car plant, I suspect

indicators.note: a suspect arrangement is a doubtful one, so the letters must be reordered
emptying part of a word removes some of its inner letters
to leave is to depart, so these letters go from what follows

parts.note: taken as written
the word with two of its inner letters emptied out

explanation.surface: A train half unloaded, just about to pull out of a motor works, perhaps carrying some fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: Take T, R and N away from 'a car plant' and the six letters left are mixed up. The car plant nods to Ford's factories.
explanation.definitionFit: Alpaca is a soft woollen fabric woven from the fleece of the llama-like South American animal.

clue.text: Pieces of fruit served up in minicab

indicators.note: served up in a down entry means sent upwards, read bottom to top
the letters sit in the next word, enclosed in its spelling

parts.note: the letters between the first and last of the word

explanation.surface: Bits of fruit handed out in the back of a taxi.
explanation.walkthrough: A minicab is a British private hire car booked by phone rather than hailed on the street.
explanation.definitionFit: Acini are the small fleshy drupelets that make up a compound fruit such as a raspberry or blackberry.

clue.text: Clergyman back working in prison

indicators.note: back means at the rear, so this piece comes last

parts.note: in the can is slang for in prison
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: A priest returns to work as a prison chaplain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in prison' gives CAN, from the slang 'in the can'; 'back' puts the working piece at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A canon is a priest attached to a cathedral chapter, so a member of the clergy.

clue.text: 12 briefly returning before 1 across

indicators.note: said briefly means cut short, so the ending is dropped
before places one piece ahead of the next
returning means going back the way it came

parts.note: twelve is a dozen, shortened to its abbreviation
the digit 1 read as the letter I
the word cut to its first two letters, as crossword references write 1ac

explanation.surface: A cross-reference puzzle within the puzzle: a shortened twelve turned round, sitting ahead of the first across answer.
explanation.walkthrough: The numbers pose as cross-references to 12 and 1 across, but they are plain numbers. A theme answer: the Ford Zodiac, a large 1950s and 1960s saloon.
explanation.definitionFit: The Zodiac was Ford of Britain's upmarket six-cylinder saloon of the 1950s and 1960s, one of the theme cars.

clue.text: Part of motorway that's Irish for street

indicators.note: one thing for another means it stands in its place

parts.note: the fast lane is the outer lane of a motorway
Ir is the abbreviation for Irish
St is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A stretch of motorway whose Irish name means street.
explanation.walkthrough: On a British motorway the fast lane is the outermost, for overtaking. A theme answer: the Ford Fairlane, a big American car of the 1950s and 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: The Fairlane was a full-size Ford sold in North America from 1955, named after Henry Ford's estate, Fair Lane.

clue.text: Perfect short clue

indicators.note: short means lacking something at the end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: ideal means perfect

explanation.walkthrough: 'Perfect' teases the Ford Prefect, a missing theme car, but it is simply the word to shorten. 'Clue' as in 'I haven't a clue'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying you have not a clue means you have no notion at all, so the two nouns are used interchangeably.

clue.text: Playing in red, Oslo keep plugging away

indicators.note: players move around a pitch, so the letters change places

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Norwegian football team in red shirts keeps grinding on.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma and the team colours make 'in red' look like kit, but it is all fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To persevere doggedly despite difficulty is to carry on, persist and continue like a weary infantryman.
